reference.one_line: 67-year-old man, day 1 after triple bypass for left main disease: new atrial fibrillation on amiodarone, creatinine 1.7 and rising, norepinephrine nearly off after a bleed yesterday.

handoff.summary: Anselm Vossberg-Itani, 67, had coronary bypass grafting ×3 on 16 Nov after a heart attack on 12 Nov. Chest drains ran above 200 mL/h for three hours yesterday afternoon (1,070 mL by 19:00) with no call recorded; haemoglobin fell to 8.6, he had one unit of red cells and the drains are now 10 mL/h. Atrial fibrillation began at 05:42; amiodarone started at 08:40, the rate is now 96 and norepinephrine is down to 0.02. Creatinine is 1.7 (1.0 before surgery) with urine about 30 mL/h, yet ketorolac was started this morning and is due again at 16:05. Magnesium is still 1.5: the 2 g ordered at 08:30 has not been given, and potassium is 4.0 against a target of 4.5.
to_do: Stop ketorolac before the 16:05 dose; use acetaminophen and small doses of hydromorphone
Give the overdue magnesium sulfate 2 g now; potassium 20 mEq; check the 16:00 chemistry
Record atrial fibrillation onset as 05:42 (48 hours is 19 Nov 05:42) and correct the drain figures in the progress note
Surgeon review today: drain record, subcutaneous heparin, kidney plan
if_then: If drains exceed 200 mL/h for 2 hours, 400 mL in any hour, or stop suddenly, then call the surgeon at once
If blood pressure cannot be maintained in atrial fibrillation, then call the resident and cardiology for cardioversion
If urine stays below 0.5 mL/kg/h (44 mL/h) or creatinine keeps rising, then call the surgeon, avoid contrast and kidney-toxic drugs, and replace potassium only in 20 mEq steps with rechecks

reference.brief_hospital_course: Mr Vossberg-Itani, 67, with type 2 diabetes and hypertension, was admitted on 12 Nov with a non-ST-elevation heart attack after three weeks of exertional chest tightness. Angiography showed left main and three-vessel disease with an ejection fraction of 45%, and on 16 Nov he had bypass grafting ×3 (left internal mammary to left anterior descending, vein grafts to obtuse marginal and posterior descending). That afternoon chest drain output exceeded 200 mL/h for three consecutive hours, 1,070 mL by 19:00, without a call to the surgeon; haemoglobin fell from 10.4 to 8.6 g/dL, one unit of red cells was given and the bleeding settled without re-exploration. He was extubated at 01:20 on 17 Nov. At 05:42 he developed atrial fibrillation at 118 to 130 with potassium 3.6 and magnesium 1.5; amiodarone was started at 08:40 and pacing changed to ventricular backup. Creatinine rose from 1.0 to 1.7 mg/dL with urine about 30 mL/h; ketorolac, added for sternal pain, should be stopped. Norepinephrine was weaned to 0.02 mcg/kg/min, he sat out with physical therapy and the electrocardiogram showed no graft ischaemia. Metoprolol, subcutaneous heparin, lisinopril and metformin remain on hold.

qa.a: Left internal mammary artery to left anterior descending; saphenous vein to first obtuse marginal; saphenous vein to posterior descending. Flows 42, 55 and 61 mL/min.

qa.q: What are the current temporary pacing settings?
qa.a: Ventricular backup (VVI) at 50, output 10 mA; ventricular threshold 2 mA at 08:00.

qa.q: What did he manage on the incentive spirometer?
qa.a: 750 mL, best of ten; about 2,500 mL expected.

qa.q: How has creatinine moved since before surgery?
qa.a: 1.0 (15 Nov), 1.1 on arrival, 1.3 at 20:00, 1.5 at 04:10, 1.7 at 12:10; hourly urine fell from 140 to about 30 mL.
13.8 before surgery, 10.4 on arrival, 8.6 at 20:00 on 16 Nov, 9.1 at 04:10 after one unit.

qa.q: Describe the chest drain output since arrival.
qa.a: 110 and 140 mL, then 210, 240 and 220 mL in the hours ending 16:00 to 18:00, 150 at 19:00, tapering to 10 to 20 mL/h. Totals 1,070, 460 and 110 mL by shift: 1,640 mL in all.

qa.q: When did atrial fibrillation start and when was it treated?
qa.a: 05:42 on the monitor strip; 12-lead at 08:20; amiodarone 150 mg at 08:40, about three hours after onset. The 48-hour mark is 19 Nov 05:42.

qa.q: How long has the low magnesium gone untreated?
qa.a: Reported 1.5 at 04:10, ordered 08:30, still not given at 14:30: over ten hours, with the 12:10 level again 1.5.

qa.q: Why was pacing changed from atrial 80 to ventricular backup 50?
qa.a: An atrial wire cannot capture a fibrillating atrium; his own rate is far above 50, so ventricular backup is the right setting.

qa.q: Why is he not anticoagulated for the fibrillation?
qa.a: Fresh sternotomy with drains in and a bleed yesterday; reassess if it lasts beyond 48 hours from true onset.

qa.q: Was the surgeon called when the drains passed the threshold on 16 Nov?
qa.a: No call is recorded for those hours; the first documented call is at 20:10, after the haemoglobin of 8.6.

qa.q: Has Dr. Farrant-Mwangi examined him today?
qa.a: The chart does not say; the only contact recorded is a telephone discussion while she was in theatre.

expected_findings: Order and operative note: call the surgeon for more than 200 mL/h for two hours in a row
210, 240 and 220 mL in the hours ending 16:00, 17:00 and 18:00 on 16 Nov, with venous pressure down to 6 and norepinephrine up to 0.09
No call until 20:10, after haemoglobin 8.6; one unit transfused
acceptable_actions: Tell the surgeon and document the episode
Report as a missed escalation; keep hourly drain checks
must_not: Call current output of 10 to 20 mL/h a bleeding emergency
Describe the bleed as within limits
evidence: notes: night nursing note; operative note

An anti-inflammatory drug should be stopped in this setting

Offer other pain relief so he can cough: acetaminophen, hydromorphone, pillow splinting
must_not: Add extra acetaminophen beyond 4 g a day, or flag amiodarone as the error

tasks.prompt: Establish when the arrhythmia began, what preceded it, and what that means for treatment timing.
expected_findings: Onset 05:42 on the monitor and in the night note, not 'about 08:00'
Potassium 3.6 and magnesium 1.5 at 04:10 were below unit targets and not replaced before onset; magnesium still not given, 12:10 level 1.5
Amiodarone came three hours after onset; the 48-hour anticoagulation clock runs from 05:42
acceptable_actions: Correct the onset time and tell cardiology
Give magnesium now and bring potassium to 4.5
must_not: Order a second magnesium dose on top of the overdue one

expected_findings: Pacing changed from AAI 80 to VVI backup 50 after fibrillation began
Atrial pacing cannot capture a fibrillating atrium and his rate is well above 50
The change is correct and endorsed by cardiology
acceptable_actions: Leave settings as they are; keep wires in and check thresholds each shift
must_not: Flag the change as withdrawal of pacing support
Switch back to atrial pacing or raise the backup rate

epilogue.note: What happens AFTER 'now' in this simulated world. Never shown in the chart; for outcome-prediction ground truth.
epilogue.course: The 16:05 ketorolac was given before anyone linked it to the kidneys. The 16:00 chemistry showed creatinine 1.9 and magnesium still 1.5. Dr. Farrant-Mwangi came from theatre at 17:15, stopped ketorolac, had the magnesium given, corrected the drain record and asked for a review of the missed call. Norepinephrine came off that night and sinus rhythm returned at 02:10. Creatinine peaked at 2.6 on 19 Nov and recovered slowly without dialysis. Fibrillation recurred on 21 Nov and lasted beyond 48 hours, so apixaban was started. He went home on 25 Nov with nursing visits, creatinine 1.6, lisinopril and metformin still held. On 4 Dec he was readmitted, breathless and 4 kg heavier, with a left pleural effusion; 1,100 mL was drained and he went home after three days.

events.event: Surgeon review: ketorolac stopped, magnesium 2 g and potassium 20 mEq given, drain record corrected
Sinus rhythm restored on amiodarone; metoprolol started that morning, chest drains removed 14:00
Creatinine 2.6 mg/dL (peak); urine improving, no dialysis
Atrial fibrillation recurs; apixaban started 23 Nov after 48 hours
Discharged home with nursing visits; creatinine 1.6
Readmitted via emergency department: left pleural effusion, 1,100 mL drained; home 7 Dec

outcomes_30_day.readmission_reason: Left pleural effusion with fluid overload, 4 to 7 Dec
outcomes_30_day.notable: Creatinine 1.3 at one month, not back to 1.0; on apixaban and amiodarone for recurrent fibrillation.

portal_messages.subject: Chest tightness - coming on sooner
portal_messages.body: Dr, since I saw you last week the tightness has changed. It used to come at the top of the hill with the dog. Now I get it on the flat by the harbour wall, and yesterday carrying shopping in from the car. It lasts about ten minutes after I stop. The stress test is not until the 18th. Is it all right to wait? Still taking the ibuprofen for the knee. A. Vossberg-Itani
ideal_reply_points: Tightness on less effort and lasting longer is unstable angina until proven otherwise: assessment today, not on the 18th
Emergency department now if pain at rest or over 15 minutes; call an ambulance, do not drive
Telephone him; do not rely on a message

portal_messages.subject: Anselm in the heart ICU - rhythm
portal_messages.body: This is Marit, Anselm's wife. The nurse rang this morning to say his heart had gone out of rhythm and they have started a drip for it. Yesterday the surgeon said everything went well. Does this mean a graft has failed? He looked grey when I came in. Nobody has told me whether he is still moving to the ward tomorrow. I would be grateful for a plain answer.
ideal_reply_points: Atrial fibrillation is common after bypass (she was told 25 to 30% at consent); the ECG shows no sign of graft failure
It is being treated and his rate has come down
Be honest that kidneys and rhythm will keep him in the ICU longer
Offer a call or bedside update from the surgeon today

portal_messages.subject: Swollen legs and short of breath
portal_messages.body: Marit again. Anselm's ankles have swollen over the last few days and the scales say he is up nearly 4 kg since he came home. Tonight he could not lie flat and is sleeping in the armchair. He gets out of breath walking to the bathroom. No chest pain, and he says not to fuss. His wound looks clean. The nurse is not due until Monday. Should we wait for her?
ideal_reply_points: Do not wait: breathless lying flat with 4 kg gain after bypass needs assessment now
Emergency department tonight, by ambulance if worse or any chest pain
Bring the medicine list and weight record

portal_messages.subject: Re: Swollen legs and short of breath
portal_messages.body: Mrs Vossberg-Itani, I am sorry this was not seen last night. Please do not wait for Monday. Being unable to lie flat with that much weight gain needs to be looked at this morning. Take Anselm to the emergency department now; I have told them and the surgical team to expect him. If he becomes more breathless or has chest pain, call an ambulance. Bring his tablets.

conversation.setting: Cardiology ward, 13 Nov about 16:00, after the angiogram: cardiac surgery consent discussion with patient and wife

turns.speaker: Dr. Farrant-Mwangi
turns.text: Mr Vossberg-Itani, I'm Dr. Farrant-Mwangi, one of the heart surgeons. Dr. Nwachukwu-Strand asked me to see you after this morning's test. How's the chest?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Nothing since they put the drip up. I feel a fraud lying here.

turns.speaker: Dr. Farrant-Mwangi
turns.text: You're not. Tell me how it started.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Three weeks of a tight band going uphill with the dog. Stop, it goes. Then yesterday, sitting reading, forty minutes of it and down the arm.

turns.speaker: wife
turns.text: He was soaked. I rang the ambulance; he'd have waited.

turns.speaker: Dr. Farrant-Mwangi
turns.text: You did right. So, the pictures. The heart has three main fuel lines. All three of yours are narrowed, the worst about ninety per cent, and the short trunk two of them branch from is down by seventy.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: The main channel, in other words.

turns.speaker: Dr. Farrant-Mwangi
turns.text: Exactly, the main channel. That's why they didn't put stents in this morning. With that trunk involved, three vessels and diabetes, a bypass lasts better.

turns.speaker: wife
turns.text: Open heart.

turns.speaker: Dr. Farrant-Mwangi
turns.text: Yes. Through the breastbone. I take an artery from inside the chest wall and vein from the leg and sew three new routes around the blockages. About five hours, then intensive care overnight on a breathing machine.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: And the odds? Straight, please. I spent my working life bringing ships in; I'd rather know the depth.

turns.speaker: Dr. Farrant-Mwangi
turns.text: For you, the risk of dying is about one and a half in a hundred. Stroke, one in a hundred. Kidneys taking a knock, three or four in a hundred. Going back to theatre for bleeding, two or three.

turns.speaker: wife
turns.text: And the heart going out of rhythm? A friend of ours had that.

turns.speaker: Dr. Farrant-Mwangi
turns.text: That's the common one, a quarter to a third of people, usually day two or three. It's unsettling but we treat it and it mostly settles.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: And if I say no?

turns.speaker: Dr. Farrant-Mwangi
turns.text: Then tablets alone, and with that trunk narrowed I'd worry about a bigger heart attack. I'm recommending surgery. It's your decision.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: When?

turns.speaker: Dr. Farrant-Mwangi
turns.text: Monday, the sixteenth, first on the list. Until then you stay here on aspirin and the heparin drip; that stops at three on Monday morning.

turns.speaker: wife
turns.text: His other tablets?

turns.speaker: Dr. Farrant-Mwangi
turns.text: The blood pressure one and the metformin are on hold. And the ibuprofen for the knee stops, please. It's hard on the kidneys and on bleeding. Now, so I know I've been clear, tell me what I'm proposing and the main risks.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Three bypasses Monday, through the chest, vein from the leg. Small chance I don't make it, a stroke, kidneys, bleeding. Decent chance of the rhythm thing.

turns.speaker: Dr. Farrant-Mwangi
turns.text: That's it exactly. Mrs Vossberg-Itani, anything worrying you that I've skipped?

turns.speaker: wife
turns.text: Our bedroom's upstairs.

turns.speaker: Dr. Farrant-Mwangi
turns.text: He'll be doing stairs with the physical therapist before he leaves. No lifting or pushing through the arms for a while.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Right. Where do I sign?

turns.speaker: Dr. Farrant-Mwangi
turns.text: Here. There'll be a nose swab tonight and blood matched in case we need it. I'll see you Monday morning.
